$comment: Where each piece of material goes. Written as it is produced, not mined later — the reasoning is freshest the day it is discovered, and a finding nobody routed is a finding nobody uses.

$destinations.landing: A section of the marketing site (docs/WEBSITE-AND-DOCS.md defines the seven).
$destinations.faq: A question a buyer or developer actually asks.
$destinations.docs: A page in the technical documentation.
$destinations.blog: Worth a post of its own — a measured finding with a reproduction that nobody else can publish.
$destinations.internal: Deliberately not published. Needs a reason.

material.what: anon could TRUNCATE every tenant table on a default Supabase project
material.angle: The strongest single artifact keelblock has. It affects every project inheriting Supabase's defaults, RLS does not cover TRUNCATE, and the reproduction is four lines.

material.what: the leading generated RLS suite confirms a total cross-tenant leak as green
material.angle: Why keelblock has two policy layers. The tool is excellent and states its own limit; the demonstration is what makes the argument.

material.what: FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY does not stop the owner on Supabase
material.angle: Corrects advice the tooling itself prints. Narrow, verifiable, useful to anyone on Supabase.

material.what: a cross-tenant write is invisible to the attacker
material.angle: Explains why read-based isolation tests cannot work, in one sentence.

material.what: a failing USING on UPDATE is a silent no-op
material.angle: Shapes every write test anyone writes here.

material.what: Cache Components break every authenticated page in Next 16
material.angle: Anyone adopting Next 16 with auth hits this. The trilemma table is the whole post.

material.what: EXECUTE on a new function defaults to PUBLIC
material.angle: One line in the tenant-table recipe.

material.what: an unconstrained INSERT policy made the access matrix cry wolf
material.angle: Our own defect, and the reason a matrix with a false positive is worse than none.

material.what: an admin could demote the owner and seize the organization
material.angle: Ours. Pairs with F-10 as the argument for auditing a suite you wrote yourself.

material.what: the last owner could orphan an organization
material.angle: Pairs with F-9.

material.what: auth.uid() reads two settings and tools clear only one
material.angle: Too specific to one tool's fixture behavior to be broadly useful; it is documented where it matters, in the gate.

material.what: a deferred constraint trigger is invisible to a statement-level test
material.angle: A correct protection no test can observe is indistinguishable from an absent one.

material.what: keelblock's own unit gate could not fail
material.angle: The most credible thing we can publish, because it is against us. Publishing it is what makes the other twenty-one believable.

material.what: an overclaimed guarantee, corrected
material.angle: Scope note on what the triggers do and do not bind.

material.what: in an app-layer model the other tenant's row is in memory before the check
material.angle: THE explanation of why keelblock exists, and a competitor wrote the code that demonstrates it.

material.what: strict CSP, static prerendering, working hydration — pick two
material.angle: Explains keelblock's report-only default, and is genuinely useful to anyone shipping a CSP on Next.

material.what: NEXT_PUBLIC_ on a credential publishes it, and nothing warns you
material.angle: Short, alarming, true, and no kit examined checks for it.

material.what: keelblock inherited two-majors-behind rot from create-next-app on day two
material.angle: The anti-rot argument, demonstrated on ourselves rather than asserted.

material.what: a gate that misreports its own failure sends you to debug the wrong thing
material.angle: Ours.

material.what: the grep-versus-parse trap, three times, by the person who gated against it
material.angle: Care demonstrably does not work; structure does. The most transferable lesson here.

material.what: a specific date, from an agency blog, in a spec
material.angle: Why the corpus exists. An unverifiable specific is more dangerous than an obvious guess.

material.what: two records of one fact disagreeing, and the gate that hid it
material.angle: Ours.

material.what: documentation that asserts a count is documentation that will lie
material.angle: The durable-versus-volatile rule, and a mechanism for it. This is the one every long-running project needs and almost none has.

material.what: a test that touches shared state is the flake that disables the suite
material.angle: Ours. Short, and the reasoning generalises to any test suite.

material.what: two tracked deferrals silently deleted while every gate said ok
material.angle: A register whose entries nothing references cannot detect its own losses. Generalises to any tracking system, and the failure is invisible by construction.

material.what: the gate protecting keelblock's flagship evidence was indifferent to what the evidence said
material.angle: The strongest self-criticism keelblock has published. A generated artifact needs two guarantees, freshness and content, and guarding only the first proves the document keeps up with the database while saying nothing about whether the database is acceptable. The fix generalizes: adjudication with a published reason, a reason floor so a token cannot retire a leak, and a stale allowance failing so the list cannot rot.

material.what: both anomalies in the published access matrix were false positives, and REACHABLE was a claim the data could not support
material.angle: Grep-versus-parse (F-20) inside a third-party tool, deciding what our own artifact says — plus the distinction between 'this assertion failed' and 'this boundary is open'. The lesson is that the word was kept loud and the dismissals were published with their reproductions, because softening a true signal to accommodate two false ones is how a matrix stops being read.

material.what: a role that could destroy a table it could not read
material.angle: The sequel to F-1 and a sharper version of it: the revoke covered two roles out of three, so service_role kept TRUNCATE on every tenant table and held no DML. Affects every project that copied the F-1 fix. Also the general rule — a hardening statement applied to the objects that existed when it was written decays silently unless ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES carries it forward.

material.what: the committed database types could not be regenerated from the repository
material.angle: A generated artifact is only evidence if it reproduces from the inputs in the repository; this one had recorded a property of one machine — pgTAP's own views, typed as part of the application schema. The failure lands on the newcomer, who is told an artifact is stale through nothing they did. Only a clean rebuild could have found it, because the gate compares the file to whatever the current stack produces.

material.what: the check that certifies every other check was a substring search
material.angle: The sharpest instance of grep-versus-parse this project has: the meta-gate enforcing 'every gate has been shown to fail' did so by looking for a word, which a TODO comment satisfies. Publishable precisely because every proof it guarded turned out to be real — the defect was that nothing could have told us otherwise.

material.what: a guarantee inherited from a platform default is a coincidence with good uptime
material.angle: The single best argument this project can make for its own thesis, and it cost one CI run to find. An assertion green on every local run failed the first time it ran anywhere else, because two builds of the same Supabase Postgres image disagree about what anon may touch. RLS still held; the layer before it did not. The F-1 fix survived the same change because it was written down rather than inherited — same repo, same class, two outcomes, one difference.
